game.title: Sudoku
game.selectCellHint: Select a cell to enter a number

step1.title: Select a cell
step1.body: Tap any empty cell on the board to select it. The row, column, and box will highlight to help you spot conflicts.

step2.title: Enter numbers
step2.body: Tap the number pad or press 1–9 on your keyboard. Enable Notes mode to pencil in candidates instead of placing a digit.

step3.title: Game tools
step3.body: Undo mistakes, get a Hint when stuck, check your solution, or pause the timer. Notes mode lets you pencil in candidates.

step4.title: Puzzle type
step4.body: Choose from 13 Sudoku variants — Classic, Diagonal, Killer, Thermo, and more. Each adds unique rules on top of standard Sudoku.

step5.title: Difficulty
step5.body: Pick Easy for a relaxed solve or Expert for a serious challenge. Difficulty controls how many clues are given.

controls.keyboard: Use keys 1-9, arrows for navigation, Backspace to clear, N for notes, Ctrl+Z/Ctrl+Y for undo/redo

NAKED_SINGLE.name: Naked Single
NAKED_SINGLE.explanation: Cell R{{row}}C{{col}} has only one possible candidate — {{value}}. All other digits are already present in its row, column, or box.

HIDDEN_SINGLE.name: Hidden Single
HIDDEN_SINGLE.explanation: Digit {{value}} can only go in cell R{{row}}C{{col}} within its house. Every other cell in that row, column, or box already rules out {{value}}.

LOCKED_CANDIDATES.name: Locked Candidates
LOCKED_CANDIDATES.explanation: A digit is confined to a single row or column within a box (or vice versa). This lets us eliminate that digit from the rest of the row, column, or box.

NAKED_PAIR.name: Naked Pair
NAKED_PAIR.explanation: Two cells in the same house share exactly the same two candidates. Those digits can be eliminated from all other cells in that house.

HIDDEN_PAIR.name: Hidden Pair
HIDDEN_PAIR.explanation: Two digits appear as candidates in exactly two cells of a house. All other candidates can be removed from those two cells.

NAKED_TRIPLE.name: Naked Triple
NAKED_TRIPLE.explanation: Three cells in a house collectively contain exactly three candidate digits. Those digits can be eliminated from the rest of the house.

HIDDEN_TRIPLE.name: Hidden Triple
HIDDEN_TRIPLE.explanation: Three digits appear in exactly three cells of a house. All other candidates can be removed from those cells.

NAKED_QUAD.name: Naked Quad
NAKED_QUAD.explanation: Four cells in a house collectively contain exactly four candidate digits. Those digits can be eliminated from the rest of the house.

HIDDEN_QUAD.name: Hidden Quad
HIDDEN_QUAD.explanation: Four digits appear in exactly four cells of a house. All other candidates can be removed from those cells.

X_WING.name: X-Wing
X_WING.explanation: A digit appears in exactly two cells in each of two rows, and those cells share the same two columns. The digit can be eliminated from those columns in all other rows.

SWORDFISH.name: Swordfish
SWORDFISH.explanation: A digit appears in exactly two or three cells across three rows, all confined to the same three columns. It can be eliminated from those columns in all other rows.

JELLYFISH.name: Jellyfish
JELLYFISH.explanation: A digit appears in two to four cells across four rows, confined to the same four columns. It can be eliminated from those columns in all other rows.

XY_WING.name: XY-Wing
XY_WING.explanation: A pivot cell with two candidates {X,Y} is connected to two pincers: one with {X,Z} and one with {Y,Z}. Any cell that sees both pincers cannot contain Z.

XYZ_WING.name: XYZ-Wing
XYZ_WING.explanation: A pivot with three candidates {X,Y,Z} is connected to two bivalue pincers that together cover all three. Z can be eliminated from cells that see all three.

W_WING.name: W-Wing
W_WING.explanation: Two bivalue cells share the same candidate pair {A,B} and are connected by a strong link on A. Digit B can be eliminated from cells that see both.

UNIQUE_RECTANGLE_1.name: Unique Rectangle Type 1
UNIQUE_RECTANGLE_1.explanation: Three corners of a rectangle contain only the same two candidates. Placing those digits in the fourth corner would create two solutions, so they must be eliminated from it.

UNIQUE_RECTANGLE_2.name: Unique Rectangle Type 2
UNIQUE_RECTANGLE_2.explanation: Two diagonal corners of a rectangle each have one extra candidate X beyond the shared pair. Since at least one must place X, it can be eliminated from cells that see both.

SIMPLE_COLORING.name: Simple Coloring
SIMPLE_COLORING.explanation: Strong links on a digit form a chain. Cells at alternating chain positions are colored. Either a color group is self-contradicting (wrap) or cells seeing both colors cannot contain the digit (trap).

ANTI_KNIGHT.name: Anti-Knight
ANTI_KNIGHT.description: Classic rules + same digits cannot be a knight's move apart

ODD_EVEN.name: Odd-Even
ODD_EVEN.description: Classic rules + marked cells must contain odd or even digits

ANTI_KING.name: Anti-King
ANTI_KING.description: Classic rules + same digits cannot be adjacent (king's move)

NON_CONSECUTIVE.name: Non-Consecutive
NON_CONSECUTIVE.description: Classic rules + adjacent cells cannot differ by 1

KROPKI.name: Kropki
KROPKI.description: Classic rules + white dot=diff 1, black dot=×2 between neighbours

KILLER.name: Killer
KILLER.description: Classic rules + cages with target sums, no digit repeats in cage

LITTLE_KILLER.name: Little Killer
LITTLE_KILLER.description: Classic rules + diagonal sums shown outside the grid (digits may repeat)

GREATER_THAN.name: Greater Than
GREATER_THAN.description: Classic rules + inequality signs between adjacent cells must be satisfied

THERMO.name: Thermo
THERMO.description: Classic rules + digits must strictly increase along each thermometer from bulb to tip

SANDWICH.name: Sandwich
SANDWICH.description: Classic rules + clues outside the grid show the sum of digits sandwiched between 1 and 9

howToPlay.title: How to Play
howToPlay.dontShowAgain: Don't show again for this variant

CLASSIC.rules: Fill the 9×9 grid so that every row, every column, and every 3×3 box contains the digits 1–9 exactly once.
CLASSIC.tip: Start with the row, column, or box that already has the most digits filled in — the fewer empty cells, the easier it is to find the missing digit.

DIAGONAL.rules:
Classic rules apply, plus both main diagonals (top-left → bottom-right and top-right → bottom-left) must each contain the digits 1–9 exactly once.

The two diagonals are highlighted in the grid.
DIAGONAL.tip: Treat each diagonal as an extra "house". A digit already placed in a cell's row, column, box, or diagonal is eliminated from all other cells on that diagonal.

WINDOKU.rules:
Classic rules apply, plus four shaded 3×3 windows must each contain the digits 1–9 exactly once.

The windows are positioned at rows 2–4 / cols 2–4, rows 2–4 / cols 6–8, rows 6–8 / cols 2–4, and rows 6–8 / cols 6–8.
WINDOKU.tip: Each window overlaps with exactly four regular 3×3 boxes. If a digit is already placed in a box that a window shares cells with, that digit is also eliminated from those shared cells in the window.

ANTI_KNIGHT.rules: Classic rules apply, plus no two cells that are a chess knight's move apart (two squares in one direction and one in the other) may contain the same digit.
ANTI_KNIGHT.tip: Each cell has up to 8 knight-move neighbours. When you place a digit, mentally eliminate it from all those neighbours — this often triggers naked singles in dense regions.

ODD_EVEN.rules:
Classic rules apply, plus:
• Cells marked with a circle must contain an odd digit (1, 3, 5, 7, or 9).
• Cells marked with a square must contain an even digit (2, 4, 6, or 8).
ODD_EVEN.tip: Process all parity constraints first — they instantly halve the candidates in marked cells, making the rest of the puzzle much easier.

ANTI_KING.rules:
Classic rules apply, plus no two cells that are a chess king's move apart (orthogonally or diagonally adjacent) may contain the same digit.

In other words, every cell has up to 8 neighbours that cannot share its digit.
ANTI_KING.tip: The king constraint is strongest in dense regions. Look for cells where many neighbours already contain the same digit — those cells are highly restricted.

NON_CONSECUTIVE.rules:
Classic rules apply, plus no two orthogonally adjacent cells (sharing an edge) may contain consecutive digits. For example, a 4 and a 5 cannot be next to each other.

Dot markers on shared borders indicate the constraint is active between those cells.
NON_CONSECUTIVE.tip: If a cell has value N, its four neighbours cannot be N−1 or N+1. Cells with value 1 or 9 are least restricted (only one forbidden neighbour value); cells with value 5 are most restricted.

KROPKI.rules:
Classic rules apply, plus dots appear between some adjacent cells:
• White dot: the two digits differ by exactly 1 (e.g. 3 and 4).
• Black dot: one digit is exactly double the other (e.g. 3 and 6).

If no dot appears between two adjacent cells, neither relationship applies.
KROPKI.tip: Black dots near 1 must be {1, 2}. Black dots near 9 are impossible (18 > 9), so eliminate 9 from those cells. Start by resolving all dot pairs before placing any other digits.

KILLER.rules:
Classic rules apply, plus cells are grouped into cages (shown by dashed outlines). Each cage has a target sum shown in its top-left corner. The digits inside a cage must:
• Sum to the target.
• Not repeat within the cage.

Note: the no-repeat rule applies within cages only, not across cages.
KILLER.tip: Add all cage totals for a complete row, column, or box (which must sum to 45). The difference tells you the sum of any cage cells that "stick out" of that unit — these are called outies and are often easy to pin down.

LITTLE_KILLER.rules:
Classic rules apply, plus numbers appear outside the grid along diagonal arrows. Each number is the sum of all digits along that diagonal direction.

Unlike Killer cages, digits may repeat along a Little Killer diagonal.
LITTLE_KILLER.tip: A diagonal that covers only 1 or 2 cells is immediately solvable. For longer diagonals, compute the minimum possible sum (all 1s) and maximum (all 9s) to narrow down the digit range.

GREATER_THAN.rules:
Classic rules apply, plus inequality signs appear between some adjacent cells. The sign always points toward the smaller digit — the cell on the open side of the sign is larger.

For example, A > B means A is greater than B.
GREATER_THAN.tip: Follow chains of inequalities to find forced minimum or maximum values. A cell that is greater than three neighbours must be at least 4; a cell less than three neighbours can be at most 6.

THERMO.rules:
Classic rules apply, plus thermometer shapes appear on the grid. Digits along each thermometer must strictly increase from the round bulb end to the pointed tip.

For example, a 4-cell thermometer could contain 2, 5, 7, 9 (each cell larger than the previous).
THERMO.tip: The longer the thermometer, the tighter the constraints. A thermometer of length N means the bulb is ≥ 1 and the tip is ≤ (10 − N). Fill in the extreme ends first.

SANDWICH.rules:
Classic rules apply, plus numbers appear outside the grid next to each row and column. Each number is the sum of the digits sandwiched between the 1 and the 9 in that row or column.

The 1 and 9 themselves are not included in the sum; only the digits between them are.
SANDWICH.tip: A clue of 0 means 1 and 9 are adjacent. A clue of 35 means all other digits (2–8) are between them. The position of 1 and 9 is the key — once you know where they are, the sandwich digits follow.
